title: DOES GOD EVER BLESS LUST? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO APPROVE
paragraphs: DOES GOD EVER BLESS LUST? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO APPROVE

Not everything that feels like love comes from God. Not every open door is His blessing. And sometimes, the very thing you are begging heaven to give you is the thing slowly pulling your heart away from Jesus.
There is a prayer that some people whisper in the darkness that they would never dare pray out loud in church.
“Lord, please let this relationship work.”
It sounds innocent.
It sounds sincere.
It even sounds spiritual.
But what if the person praying already knows the relationship is built on something God has forbidden?
What if there are messages being deleted, boundaries being crossed, promises being broken, and a conscience that has been begging for attention?
What if the prayer really means, “God, please bless what I am not willing to surrender”?
And here is the question that may hurt more than you expect.
What if you are not waiting for God's blessing at all? What if you are waiting for God to stop confronting what you already know is wrong?
Before you close this article, understand something.
This is not written to humiliate the person who fell into sexual sin.
It is not written to tell the struggling believer that Jesus has abandoned them.
It is not written to make the wounded feel unworthy of love.
It is written because there are people who have mistaken intense desire for divine confirmation, sexual chemistry for covenant love, and temporary pleasure for God's approval.
And some of them are quietly losing themselves.
Maybe one of them is you.
Maybe you never intended to go this far.
It began with a conversation.
Someone noticed you.
Someone listened when nobody else seemed interested.
Someone made you feel attractive after years of feeling invisible.
And something inside you came alive.
At first, you told yourself it was harmless.
Then the conversations became private.
The private conversations became emotional dependence.
The emotional dependence became physical intimacy.
And somewhere between the first compromise and the last deleted message, you stopped asking whether God was pleased.
You started asking whether God would understand.
He does understand your weakness.
But understanding your weakness is not the same as blessing your disobedience.
And that distinction may save your soul from years of unnecessary heartbreak.
Jesus said something that exposes the human heart with frightening precision.
In Matthew 5:28, He taught:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.” (KJV)
The original Greek contains the expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn).
In this context, it speaks of looking at someone with the purpose of lusting after that person.
Notice what Jesus was confronting.
He was not declaring that recognizing someone's beauty is automatically adultery.
He was not saying that every involuntary thought or unwanted temptation makes a person guilty of deliberately committing sexual sin.
He was exposing the heart that intentionally cultivates forbidden desire.
The heart that does not merely notice.
It entertains.
It imagines.
It feeds.
It returns.
It makes room for what it knows it should refuse.

The Greek verb epithymeō, from which this expression comes, refers to desiring or longing for something. Desire itself is not automatically sinful; its moral character depends on what is desired and how that desire is directed.

But when desire turns another human being into an object of selfish gratification, when it seeks what God has forbidden, when it becomes willing to betray faithfulness and holiness for pleasure, Scripture calls us to confront it.
Jesus was not merely interested in whether your body crossed a line.
He was concerned with what your heart was becoming before your body ever moved.
And that should make all of us examine ourselves.
Because a person can appear respectable in public while privately nurturing fantasies that are destroying their spiritual life.
A marriage can look beautiful in photographs while one spouse secretly gives their imagination to someone else.
A believer can sing worship songs on Sunday while spending the rest of the week feeding desires they refuse to surrender.
And yes, a person can sincerely love Jesus while struggling with lust.
But loving Jesus means learning to bring even our most uncomfortable struggles into His light.
Not hiding them behind religious language.
Not defending them with emotional excuses.
Not baptizing them with the word love.
Here is where the question becomes unavoidable.
Does God ever bless lust?
If by lust we mean sinful sexual desire that contradicts God's will, the biblical answer is no.
God does not bless lust as lust.
He does not declare sin righteous because the emotions are powerful.
He does not change His holiness because two people feel deeply connected.
James 1:13–15 explains that God does not tempt anyone with evil, and that sinful desire, when embraced and allowed to grow, gives birth to sin, which leads toward death.
The original Greek of James 1:14 uses the word ἐπιθυμίας (epithymias), meaning desire or craving.
James describes a progression.
Desire becomes an enticement.
Enticement is embraced.
Sin develops.
And sin, when allowed to run its course, produces death.
Not every desire is evil, but desire directed toward sin can become a powerful trap.
And one of the most dangerous things about lust is that it rarely introduces itself as destruction.
It often arrives disguised as comfort.
As affection.
As being understood.
As finally feeling wanted.
It may even whisper, “You deserve to be happy.”
But happiness cannot be the ultimate judge of holiness.
You can feel happy while betraying someone.
You can feel wanted while being used.
You can feel emotionally alive while spiritually becoming numb.
And you can experience pleasure in something that is slowly destroying your integrity.
The existence of pleasure does not prove the presence of God's approval.
Read that again.
The existence of pleasure does not prove the presence of God's approval.
There is a difference between God's kindness in allowing you to experience good things and God's moral approval of everything you choose to do with them.
Jesus taught that the Father gives sunlight and rain to both the evil and the good (Matthew 5:45).
God's generosity is real.
But receiving something pleasant is not proof that every decision surrounding it is righteous.
A relationship may begin in sinful circumstances and later become a lawful marriage.
A child may be conceived through an act of sexual sin and still possess immeasurable dignity as a human being made in God's image.
A person may encounter Christ in the middle of a morally broken situation and experience genuine redemption.
None of those truths means God blessed the original sin.
They mean His mercy is greater than the wreckage human sin can create.
And perhaps that is the distinction somebody desperately needs to hear.
God can bring good out of what was sinful without ever calling the sin good.
Think about David.
A king.
A worshiper.
A man entrusted with extraordinary responsibility.
And yet, in 2 Samuel 11, David saw Bathsheba, desired her, took her, and then attempted to conceal the consequences.
The biblical account makes clear that David abused his royal power. Bathsheba should not be casually blamed as though the text portrays two equally powerful participants in a romantic affair.
David was the king.
He sent for her.
He committed adultery.
And when the consequences threatened his reputation, he arranged circumstances that led to her husband Uriah's death.
What began with desire became exploitation, deception, and bloodshed.
David's position did not excuse him.
His previous worship did not excuse him.
His spiritual history did not excuse him.
And when the prophet Nathan confronted him, David could no longer hide behind his crown.
He confessed.
“I have sinned against the LORD.” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
Those words matter.
Not because they erased every earthly consequence.
They did not.
But because David finally stopped defending what God was confronting.
Psalm 51 preserves the language of a deeply repentant heart.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The Hebrew verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from bara, meaning “to create.”
David was not merely asking God to help him maintain a cleaner public image.
He was pleading for inward renewal.
He needed more than damage control.
He needed a heart transformed by God.
And perhaps that is the prayer you have been avoiding.
Not “Lord, make this relationship work.”
Not “Lord, help me keep this secret.”
Not “Lord, make the guilt disappear.”
But...
“Lord, create in me a clean heart, even if that means surrendering something I desperately want.”
Because repentance is not simply feeling terrible after sin.
It is turning toward God with a willingness to abandon what dishonors Him.
And sometimes that turning is painful.
Sometimes it means deleting the conversation.
Sometimes it means ending an affair.
Sometimes it means telling the truth to someone you have deceived.
Sometimes it means asking for accountability instead of another opportunity to hide.
Sometimes it means admitting that what you called love was actually a mixture of loneliness, attraction, insecurity, and selfishness.
And sometimes it means realizing that you have been using another human being to medicate wounds only God can ultimately heal.
But hear this carefully.
God is not asking you to despise your body.
He created it.
He is not asking you to pretend attraction does not exist.
He designed human beings with the capacity for affection, intimacy, and marital desire.
Scripture does not teach that all sexual desire is dirty.
In Genesis 2:24, the union of husband and wife is presented as part of God's design.
In the Song of Songs, marital love and attraction are celebrated through poetry.
And Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage while warning against sexual immorality and adultery.
The problem is not that God created desire.
The problem is what sin does when desire refuses God's boundaries.
God's design for sexual intimacy is not a declaration that pleasure is evil.
It is a declaration that intimacy matters too much to be reduced to appetite.
A human being is not a product to consume.
A spouse is not an object to possess.
Another person's loneliness is not an invitation to exploit them.
And someone else's marriage is not a territory for your emotions to conquer.
Love seeks the good of another person.
Lust is willing to sacrifice that good to satisfy itself.
Love can wait when waiting is right.
Lust insists that waiting is unbearable.
Love respects a person's dignity.
Lust can reduce a person to what they provide.
Love tells the truth.
Lust often depends on secrecy.
These are not perfect diagnostic tests for every human emotion, but they reveal a serious moral difference.
And now I want to speak to the person who has already crossed the line.
The person reading this with a tightening chest.
The person remembering a hotel room.
A private message.
A hidden photograph.
A promise made to someone else.
A moment when you knew you should stop, but you continued anyway.
You may be thinking, “Is there still hope for me?”
Yes.
There is hope.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Not because the consequences are imaginary.
Not because repentance will automatically restore every broken relationship.
There is hope because Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And that includes people with sexual histories they wish they could erase.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8:1–11.

The account is traditionally included in John's Gospel, although the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts do not contain this passage and its textual history is disputed. It should therefore not carry the entire weight of a doctrine that is established elsewhere in Scripture.
Still, the scene as traditionally received has powerfully reminded generations of Christians of both mercy and holiness.
A woman stands accused of adultery.
Her shame is public.
Her accusers are ready to condemn.
Jesus challenges the self-righteousness of those who would stone her.
And the account concludes with His call:
“Go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Notice the balance.
Jesus did not treat her as disposable.
But neither did He celebrate adultery.
Mercy was not permission to continue.
Grace was an invitation to a different life.
That same union of grace and truth appears throughout the New Testament.
Jesus welcomes sinners.
He calls them to repentance.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
And He does not require a person to become flawless before coming to Him.
The cross is where sinners find mercy, not a trophy reserved for those who never struggled.
But the grace that forgives also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
So if you are caught in pornography, secret fantasies, sexual compromise, or a relationship you know violates God's commands, do not mistake your struggle for proof that Jesus has rejected you.
Bring it into the light.
Confess honestly to God.
Seek trusted, mature support.
If you are caught in a cycle of compulsive behavior, wise pastoral care and qualified professional help can work alongside spiritual discipleship.
If you have harmed another person, take responsibility without demanding immediate forgiveness or reconciliation.
And if you are being pressured, coerced, threatened, or abused, understand that another person's wrongdoing is not your guilt. Seek safety and appropriate support.
Jesus does not call the wounded to remain in danger.
And repentance must never become an excuse for someone else to control or exploit you.
The apostle Paul wrote something remarkable to the Corinthian believers.
After naming serious sins, including sexual immorality and adultery, he said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
And such were some of you.
Those words carry a future that shame cannot imagine.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have to become the permanent definition of your identity.
Paul did not say that the Corinthians had never sinned.
He said that God's saving work had changed their standing and called them into a new life.
The Greek text includes the words ἀπελούσασθε, ἡγιάσθητε, and ἐδικαιώθητε.
Apelousasthe. You were washed.
Hēgiasthēte. You were sanctified.
Edikaiōthēte. You were justified.
These are not empty religious decorations.
They speak of cleansing, being set apart for God, and being declared righteous through the saving work of Christ.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a program for improving your behavior.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Our hope rests in Him.
Not in our ability to manufacture a spotless history.
Not in our power to erase consequences.
Not in our determination to never experience temptation again.
In Him.
And because we belong to Him, our lives are no longer meant to be surrendered to whatever desire shouts the loudest.
Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
“Flee fornication.” (KJV)
The underlying Greek command is φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not build a comfortable apartment beside it.
Not keep an emergency entrance open in case loneliness returns.
Flee.
This does not mean every struggle is solved by one dramatic decision.
Some patterns require sustained repentance, accountability, healing, and the patient renewal of the mind.
But Scripture does not encourage believers to make peace with the very thing they are called to leave.
And there is a reason.
Because what you repeatedly feed becomes harder to resist.
A secret relationship may begin to feel necessary.
Pornography may train the imagination to treat people as consumable images.
Unrestrained fantasy may make faithfulness feel less satisfying.
And unchecked sexual entitlement can gradually weaken empathy, honesty, and self-control.
Not everyone experiences these patterns in the same way, but their potential for spiritual and relational harm is serious.
The question is not merely, “Can I get away with this?”
It is, “What is this doing to the person I am becoming?”
What is it doing to your prayer life?
Your honesty?
Your marriage?
Your ability to see others as people rather than instruments of pleasure?
Your willingness to obey Jesus when obedience costs you something?
And here is a question that may stay with you tonight.
If God answered every prayer you prayed for the thing you lust after, would it actually draw you closer to Christ?
Or would it simply make your compromise easier to continue?
Because sometimes we ask God for confirmation when He has already given us instruction.
We search for signs.
We replay coincidences.
We interpret every unexpected message as destiny.
We say, “If this relationship is wrong, why does it feel so right?”
But strong feelings are not infallible spiritual guidance.
A door opening does not automatically mean God wants you to walk through it.
And a door closing does not automatically mean God is punishing you.
Scripture, wise counsel, honest examination, and prayerful discernment matter far more than treating every emotional experience as a message from heaven.
God's will does not become righteous or unrighteous based on how intense our feelings are.
And there is another truth we cannot avoid.
Sometimes the thing you call a blessing is actually a test of what you are willing to obey.
That does not mean we can confidently identify every hardship or temptation as a specific test sent by God.
James 1:13 expressly rejects the idea that God tempts people toward evil.
But the circumstances of life can expose where our loyalties stand.
When desire and obedience collide, what will govern your decision?
Your appetite?
Your fear of being alone?
Your need for attention?
Or your trust in Jesus?
I know that sounds easier on a screen than it feels in a lonely bedroom.
I know there are people who have gone years without tenderness.
People who are married but feel emotionally abandoned.
People who have been rejected so often that being desired feels like oxygen.
People who grew up learning that affection always came with conditions.
People whose earliest experiences of intimacy were marked by betrayal or abuse.
For some, sexual temptation is tangled with deep emotional pain.
And it would be cruel to pretend that one sentence can untangle years of suffering.
But it would also be cruel to tell you that the only answer to your pain is to keep feeding a desire that may wound you further.
Jesus does not minimize the pain beneath the temptation.
He invites you to bring the pain to Him.
Not as a performance.
Not as a polished testimony.
But as you are.
Exhausted.
Confused.
Ashamed.
Lonely.
Afraid of losing the person you have become attached to.
Afraid that holiness will mean never being loved.
Listen.
Obedience to Christ is not a sentence to a loveless life.
Marriage is a good gift, but it is not guaranteed to every believer.
Singleness is not spiritual failure.
And neither marriage nor sexual fulfillment can bear the weight of being someone's savior.
Jesus is enough to be our ultimate hope, even when our emotional lives remain difficult and our desires are not immediately fulfilled.
That truth does not erase loneliness.
It gives loneliness somewhere holy to go.
And perhaps the most beautiful evidence of God's grace is not that every temptation disappears overnight.
Perhaps it is that a person who once could not imagine saying no begins, by the Spirit's help, to choose faithfulness.
One honest confession.
One boundary restored.
One relationship ended.
One act of repentance.
One day without returning to the old hiding place.
Then another.
Not earning salvation.
Not purchasing God's affection.
But learning to live as someone who has been redeemed.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It does not declare sin harmless.
It declares that condemnation does not have the final word over those who belong to the Savior.
And Romans 8 goes on to describe life through the Spirit, including the putting to death of sinful deeds.
Grace and transformation belong together.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior has never been that your scandal is beautiful.
Sin is not beautiful.
Betrayal is not beautiful.
Exploitation is not beautiful.
The destruction of trust is not beautiful.
But the grace of Jesus Christ can reach people in the middle of what is broken and begin something they never thought possible.
That is the miracle.
Not that God changes the definition of sin to make us comfortable.
But that He can change sinners through the Gospel.
From hiding to confession.
From deception to truth.
From bondage to growing freedom.
From spiritual numbness to renewed surrender.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by guaranteeing that every consequence disappears.
But by making redemption possible through His death and resurrection.
And if you have read this far, perhaps you recognize something.
You were not merely searching for an answer about lust.
You were searching for permission.
Or forgiveness.
Or hope.
Or the courage to walk away.
Maybe you wanted someone to tell you that God understands your circumstances so completely that He will make an exception for what Scripture calls sin.
He understands your circumstances more completely than anyone ever could.
But He loves you too deeply to call darkness light.
And He is merciful enough to receive the person who finally stops pretending.
You do not need to publish the details of your struggle for strangers to examine.
You do not need to expose another person's private history in a comment section.
But if this message has reached a place you have kept hidden, consider taking one honest step today.
And if you need prayer but do not know what to say, “Pray for me” is enough.
You are not required to disclose your private wounds to belong in a community of believers.
Sometimes the bravest thing a struggling Christian can say is, “I need help.”
And if this article brought a name to your mind, someone caught in compromise, someone quietly drowning in shame, someone convinced they are too far gone, consider sending it to them privately.
Not to accuse them.
Not to embarrass them.
But to remind them that truth and mercy still meet in Jesus Christ.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable.
But because there may come a night when you are tempted to confuse longing with love again, and you need to remember that God has not called you to be ruled by your desires.
Behind every article, every resource, every message of encouragement, and every effort to reach another struggling soul is the ongoing work of creating, maintaining, and sharing Christian content.
Our desire is to keep that biblical nourishment accessible and to expand the reach of these resources to more people.
Scripture says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
The context teaches willing, purposeful generosity rather than giving under compulsion.
You do not need to pay for God's forgiveness.
You cannot purchase His favor.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
More biblical nourishment.
More encouragement for people wrestling with sin.
More resources for believers learning to follow Jesus faithfully.
More opportunities to tell someone that their past does not have to be the end of their story.
Because Christ did not die to create a marketplace for mercy.
He died and rose again to save sinners.
And now, before you move on, return with me to that first prayer.
“Lord, please let this relationship work.”
Maybe after reading this, you need to pray something different.
“Lord, if this relationship is honoring You, teach us to walk in purity, honesty, and faithfulness.
But if I am asking You to bless something You have forbidden, give me the courage to stop.
If I have wounded someone, teach me to take responsibility.
If I have been using another person to escape my emptiness, heal what I have been afraid to face.
If I have made pleasure my master, teach me to love You more than my appetites.
And if shame has convinced me that I am beyond Your mercy, lead me back to the cross.
Create in me a clean heart, O God.
Not merely a better reputation.
Not merely stronger willpower.
A clean heart.
In Jesus' name.
Amen.”
There may still be consequences to face.
There may still be conversations you dread.
There may still be tears.
And the road toward restoration may be longer than you wish.
But do not confuse the pain of repentance with the absence of grace.
Sometimes telling the truth hurts because a lie has been allowed to live too long.
Sometimes surrender feels like loss because we have grown attached to something that was never meant to rule us.
And sometimes the first step toward freedom is the moment you stop asking God to protect your compromise and begin asking Him to transform your heart.
Does God ever bless lust?
No.
But He welcomes repentant sinners.
He forgives through Jesus Christ.
He gives His Spirit to His people.
He teaches them to walk in holiness.
And He can redeem lives that seem hopelessly entangled in shame.
The greatest blessing is not getting everything your desires demand.
It is belonging to Jesus Christ, even when following Him means surrendering something you thought you could never live without.
So tonight, if you are standing between the desire you have been feeding and the Savior who is calling you, remember this:
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could learn to hide your chains more beautifully. He came to redeem you, so those chains would no longer be your master.
